source.title_on_document: Impacto de la Inteligencia Artificial Generativa sobre la Originalidad Creativa y el Pensamiento Proyectual en Estudiantes de Diseño Gráfico

paper_design_summary: Ninety-six university graphic design students in existing course sections (paralelos) formed a control group (n = 48) and an experimental group (n = 48); assignment was not random. Over eight weeks both groups did the same design project activities, but the experimental group got generative-AI training (week 2) and used ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL-E and Adobe Firefly in weeks 3 to 6, while the control group worked without AI. Two external blinded evaluators scored creative originality (composite rubric: novelty, flexibility, elaboration, utility) and design thinking with 1-5 analytic rubrics at pretest and posttest; groups were compared with ANOVA on posttest scores.

studies.label: Quasi-experiment, graphic design students, AI vs conventional design strategies (8 weeks)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL-E, Adobe Firefly) plus AI training versus conventional design strategies without AI; groups were existing course sections.
assignment.quote: la asignación a los grupos control y experimental no fue aleatoria, sino determinada por los paralelos ya existentes de la asignatura, lo que corresponde a un diseño cuasi experimental
assignment.locator: p. 1180 (PDF p. 15), Limitaciones; also p. 1172 (PDF p. 7), Materiales y métodos: 'manteniendo la organización natural de los grupos académicos'

arms.name: Experimental
arms.description: Same course contents and activities; generative-AI training in week 2 and use of ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL-E and Adobe Firefly for research, ideation, generating alternatives and conceptual development in weeks 3 to 6.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Same contents, activities, objectives and evaluation criteria, carried out with conventional design strategies without AI assistance.

participants.exclusions: Exclusion criteria stated (repeated non-attendance, dropping out, incomplete evaluation instruments; inclusion required at least 80 percent attendance), but the paper does not report how many students were excluded. The sample of 96 is the final sample; ANOVA df (1, 94) match 96.
participants.who: University students enrolled in the Graphic Design program, one course, one institution; convenience (non-probabilistic) sample; 54.2 percent female, 62.5 percent aged 18-21.
participants.country: not_stated (authors at Ecuadorian universities; the institution of the sample is not named)
participants.quote: La muestra quedó conformada por 96 estudiantes, distribuidos equitativamente en un grupo control (n = 48) y un grupo experimental (n = 48).
participants.locator: p. 1172 (PDF p. 7), Materiales y métodos; p. 1175-1176 (PDF pp. 10-11), Table 4

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL-E, Adobe Firefly (versions not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: Mix of chatbot and text-to-image tools used as support for research, ideation, generation of alternatives and conceptual development of design projects (weeks 3-6, Table 1 'Ideación asistida por IA' in week 4). AI use was recorded by self-report (p. 1180).

task.description: Graphic design course project: problem research, AI-assisted (experimental) or conventional ideation, conceptual development, graphic proposals, critical evaluation; creative originality and design thinking scored by rubric at pretest and posttest.
task.duration: Eight weeks (pretest week 1, AI training week 2, AI use weeks 3-6, critical evaluation week 7, posttest and focus groups week 8); p. 1173 (PDF p. 8), Table 1

outcomes.name: Originalidad creativa (creative originality, composite rubric score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Analytic rubric, 1-5 scale, four dimensions (novelty, flexibility, elaboration, utility) following Runco and Jaeger (2012); scored double-blind by two external evaluators ('evaluadores externos', 'jueces externos'; their expertise is not described). ICC = .98, exact agreement 96.9 percent. Only the composite is reported; no dimension-level results. ANCOVA with pretest as covariate reported only in words ('practically identical').

contrasts.reported: Posttest: Control 2.65 ± 0.45, Experimental 4.12 ± 0.58 (pretest: Control 2.52 ± 0.40, Experimental 2.56 ± 0.44); n = 48 per group. ANOVA F = 170.51, gl = 1, 94, p < .001, η² = 0.65. Pretest equivalence: Levene F = 0.05, p = .828; t = 0.18, p = .857; Mann-Whitney p = .812.
contrasts.locator: p. 1176 (PDF p. 11), Table 5 and pretest-equivalence paragraph; p. 1177 (PDF p. 12), Table 6; group n in Table 4 (pp. 1175-1176)

outcomes.name: Pensamiento proyectual (design thinking, composite rubric score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Design-process quality: analytic rubric, 1-5 scale, four dimensions (research, conceptualization, ideation, evaluation); scored double-blind by the same two external evaluators. ICC = .94, exact agreement 90.6 percent. Only the composite is reported.

contrasts.reported: Posttest: Control 2.58 ± 0.40, Experimental 4.05 ± 0.61 (pretest: Control 2.45 ± 0.35, Experimental 2.51 ± 0.41); n = 48 per group. ANOVA F = 186.57, gl = 1, 94, p < .001, η² = 0.67. Pretest equivalence: Levene F = 0.15, p = .696; t = -0.65, p = .515; Mann-Whitney p = .623.
contrasts.locator: p. 1176 (PDF p. 11), Table 5; p. 1177 (PDF p. 12), Table 6

eligibility.reason: Groups were intact course sections, not randomly assigned (p. 1180, Limitaciones; p. 1179 'sin aleatorización'). The study has 96 students analyzed and rubric scores of creative originality by two external blinded evaluators, so criteria 2 and 3 are met. It is a quasi_people design, which the dataset folds into observational context. The experimental group also got AI training the control group did not (p. 1180).

one_line_finding: In a non-randomized comparison of 96 graphic design students, the section that used generative AI scored higher on rubric-rated creative originality at posttest (4.12 vs 2.65 on 1-5; F(1, 94) = 170.51, p < .001, η² = 0.65; pp. 1176-1177, Tables 5-6).
open_questions: Whether AI was available when the scored posttest output was produced is not fully clear: AI use ran in weeks 3-6 (Table 1 note, p. 1173) and the posttest was applied in week 8, but the Discussion (p. 1179) says the rubric focused on the final proposals ('propuestas finales'), which were developed during the AI weeks. Coded with_ai / yes on that reading.
The paper does not say what output was rated at pretest (week 1) or whether the pretest and posttest tasks were the same design brief.
Expertise of the two external evaluators is not described; coded expert_raters as the closest fit.
The country and institution of the sample are not named; author affiliations are Ecuadorian (UISEK Quito, UNACH Riobamba).
notes: Mixed-methods sequential explanatory design; focus groups (n = 24) produced themes including a 'latent risk of aesthetic homogenization' (Table 7, p. 1178), but no diversity outcome was measured. Likert instruments for AI use and 'expanded creativity' were lost and the planned PLS-SEM was not run (pp. 1171, 1180-1181). The paper reports Spearman rho = .73 between originality and design thinking at posttest (p. 1178), which is not a contrast. The authors note the effect size is much larger than in the literature and than in earlier versions of the manuscript (p. 1177, p. 1179). Journal page numbers are given with PDF page numbers (PDF p. = journal p. - 1165).
